cards.front: Why can developing neurons die even after their axons reach a target?
cards.back: The target supplies a limited amount of survival factor. Neurons that fail to obtain enough of the right factor die.
cards.quote: a target makes a limited amount of a survival factor, and neurons that fail to get enough die.

cards.front: Name the four mammalian neurotrophins.
cards.back: NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and NT-4.
cards.quote: NGF is one of four mammalian neurotrophins: NGF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), neurotrophin-3 (NT-3) and neurotrophin-4 (NT-4).

cards.front: A protein made of two identical chains, as each mammalian neurotrophin is, is a {{c1::dimer}}.
cards.quote: Each is a dimer, two identical chains held together, and all four share one fold.

cards.front: Which receptor family includes p75, the shared neurotrophin receptor?
cards.back: The TNF-receptor family; p75 has no kinase.
cards.quote: It belongs to the family of the tumour necrosis factor (TNF) receptor, and it is a relative of Fas, the death receptor from that lesson.

cards.front: How can proteolysis convert a longer secreted protein precursor into its mature form?
cards.back: Proteases remove its extra pro-domain, leaving the mature protein.
cards.quote: the pro-domain, which proteases cut off to leave the mature protein.

cards.front: Why does detecting p75 alone fail to establish whether a neurotrophin will kill a cell?
cards.back: Its effect depends on the whole receptor balance: it can cooperate with TrkA, while p75 with sortilin can mediate precursor-induced death.
cards.quote: What p75 does depends on its partners: with TrkA it can work alongside the kinase,

cards.front: NGF preferentially activates the receptor tyrosine kinase {{c1::TrkA}}.
cards.quote: A neuron that makes TrkA is switched on by NGF, one that makes TrkC by NT-3.
cards.section: How a Trk receptor turns on

cards.front: NT-3 preferentially activates the receptor tyrosine kinase {{c1::TrkC}}.
cards.back: NT-3 can also activate TrkA and TrkB more weakly.
cards.quote: A neuron that makes TrkA is switched on by NGF, one that makes TrkC by NT-3.
cards.section: How a Trk receptor turns on

cards.front: How does a neurotrophin dimer activate Trk receptor tyrosine kinases?
cards.back: The dimer brings two receptors together. Their kinase domains phosphorylate each other on tyrosines, creating docking sites for survival signaling.
cards.quote: Their kinase domains, now side by side, phosphorylate each other on tyrosines, as in the lesson on receptor tyrosine kinases.
cards.section: How a Trk receptor turns on

cards.front: Which two survival signaling branches begin at phosphorylated Trk docking sites?
cards.back: Ras to ERK and PI3K to Akt.
cards.quote: the Ras to ERK cascade (that lesson) and the PI3K to Akt route (that lesson).
cards.section: How a Trk receptor turns on

cards.front: A dimeric growth factor brings two receptor tyrosine kinases together, but their kinase domains cannot phosphorylate tyrosines. What happens to recruitment of survival signaling proteins, and why?
cards.back: Recruitment through those docking sites is impaired: receptor pairing alone cannot create the phosphorylated tyrosines that recruit the survival signaling machinery.
cards.quote: The phosphorylated tyrosines become docking sites that start two survival branches you have met:
cards.section: How a Trk receptor turns on

cards.front: Why did cloning p75 leave the high-affinity NGF receptor unidentified?
cards.back: p75 bound NGF with low affinity and lacked a kinase. Alone, it could not explain the higher-affinity sites observed on neurons.
cards.quote: Neurons were known to have higher-affinity sites as well, and on its own p75 could not account for them.

cards.front: How can a cancer-associated fusion bypass a receptor kinase’s normal need for a ligand?
cards.back: The fusion can keep the kinase active without ligand binding.
cards.quote: The fusion kept the kinase on without any ligand.

cards.front: A previously NGF-unresponsive fibroblast is given normal TrkA. NGF then binds TrkA, induces its tyrosine phosphorylation and stimulates division without p75. What is TrkA sufficient for in this system?
cards.back: TrkA is sufficient to confer an NGF response in these fibroblasts without p75. This establishes sufficiency in that cell system.
cards.quote: Barbacid's group also found that fibroblasts carrying Trk divided in response to NGF without needing p75.

cards.front: What does a gene knockout do to the targeted gene’s functional product?
cards.back: It disrupts the gene so that no working protein, or no working form of that protein, is made.
cards.quote: a chosen gene, or part of it, has been disrupted so that it makes no working protein, or no working form of one protein.

cards.front: In a developing ganglion, a receptor knockout initially has a normal cell count. Later, cell counts fall, mitotic figures remain unchanged and shrunken, condensed nuclei increase. Which receptor role does this support?
cards.back: A role in survival after neurons form. The initial population forms, division does not fall, and evidence of cell death increases.
cards.quote: Over those embryonic ages, dividing cells (mitotic figures) were no fewer than in controls, while dying cells, with shrunken, condensed (pyknotic) nuclei, increased.

cards.front: Which neuronal groups are reduced in mice lacking NGF or TrkA?
cards.back: Sympathetic neurons and many small sensory neurons that sense pain and heat.
cards.quote: "Lost" means fewer neurons: usually part of a ganglion survives,

cards.front: A mouse loses TrkC function. Which sensory deficit would explain abnormal limb positioning, and why?
cards.back: Reduced proprioceptive input: NT-3–TrkC supports afferents that report limb position, and mice lacking either lose these neurons.
cards.quote: Each factor-receptor pair has its own pattern of loss, though deleting a factor and its main receptor removes many of the same neurons.

cards.front: A BDNF-null mouse has fewer neurons sensing head movement. Which affected sensory population explains this, and why?
cards.back: Vestibular neurons. BDNF deletion reduces this population, which senses balance and head movement.
cards.quote: The four factors share a fold and a co-receptor, but to a neuron they are separate signals.

cards.front: Which visceral sensory neuron population is reduced by deleting either BDNF or NT-4 in mice?
cards.back: Nodose-petrosal neurons, which carry signals from the heart, lungs and gut.
cards.quote: The map has overlaps like this, and some populations need more than one factor at different stages.

cards.front: A mouse knockout removes the kinase-containing form of TrkB. Would restricting the search for neuronal loss to peripheral ganglia capture its full reported distribution?
cards.back: No. Neuronal loss occurs in both the central and peripheral nervous systems, so the search must include both.
cards.quote: Deleting each neurotrophin or Trk gene in mice, one at a time, sorts the family by which neurons are lost.

cards.front: In a matched mouse ganglion, removing NT-3 causes greater neuron loss than removing TrkC. How can NT-3’s receptor preferences explain the difference?
cards.back: NT-3 deletion also removes its weaker support through TrkA and TrkB; TrkC deletion removes only its TrkC route. The size of the difference depends on the ganglion, age and TrkC form deleted.
cards.quote: Removing TrkC takes away only NT-3's action through TrkC, while removing NT-3 also takes away its weaker help through TrkA and TrkB.

cards.front: An NT-3-null ganglion at birth has fewer neurons than a TrkC-null ganglion sampled earlier. How would you test whether the difference reflects NT-3 support through other Trks?
cards.back: Compare the same ganglion at the same age and specify the TrkC form deleted. Greater loss without NT-3 would be consistent with lost TrkA/TrkB support. Rules: NT-3 uses several Trks, and knockout differences depend on ganglion, age and deleted form.
cards.quote: the size of the gap depends on the ganglion, the age and which form of TrkC was deleted.

cards.front: Blocking NGF with an antibody reduces cell death in developing chick retina. What does this show about the source and role of NGF in that experiment?
cards.back: The tissue’s own NGF contributes to death; the effect does not require adding NGF to the tissue.
cards.quote: In the retina the NGF was the tissue's own: an antibody to NGF reduced the death.

cards.front: Why does sortilin help p75 bind proNGF tightly?
cards.back: Sortilin grips the pro-domain while p75 grips the mature part, allowing the receptor pair to hold the precursor tightly.
cards.quote: Sortilin grips the pro-domain while p75 grips the mature part of the factor, so the pair can hold the precursor tightly.

cards.front: In the cultured-cell experiments, was conversion of proNGF to mature NGF required for p75-mediated apoptosis?
cards.back: No. An uncleavable precursor still kills, showing that cleavage is unnecessary for this death signal in the tested cells.
cards.quote: A precursor that cannot be cut still kills, so it does not need to be trimmed first.

cards.front: A secreted precursor kills one cell type; its mature product supports another. Design a test of whether cleavage is necessary for killing while controlling for dose and cell type.
cards.back: Test uncleavable precursor, cleavable precursor and mature protein at matched concentrations within each cell type. Killing by uncleavable precursor shows cleavage is unnecessary. Rules: processing changes ligand form, and receptor context changes cellular response.
cards.quote: mutate its cut sites so that proteases cannot trim it, and compare it with mature NGF at the same concentration.

cards.front: Why does proNGF-induced death in cultured neurons fail to establish its contribution to normal developmental neuron loss?
cards.back: The amount of uncut precursor reaching neurons during normal development and its contribution to developmental death remain uncertain.
cards.quote: How much it contributes to the normal deaths of development is less clear.

cards.front: The same proNGF preparation is applied to two cultures: one has abundant p75 and sortilin but little TrkA; the other is dominated by TrkA. Should the response be identical? Explain.
cards.back: No. The p75–sortilin-rich culture is more likely to die; TrkA-dominated cells may show survival. Outcome depends on receptor balance, and precursor responses have differed between experiments.
cards.quote: so the outcome depends on the cell's balance of TrkA, p75 and sortilin.

cards.front: For simple ligand binding, Kd is the free ligand concentration at which {{c1::half}} of that class of binding sites is occupied.
cards.quote: Kd is the free concentration at which half the sites are occupied.

cards.front: In a simple ligand-binding model, high-affinity sites have Kd = 10 pM and low-affinity sites Kd = 1 nM. At 100 pM free ligand, calculate occupancy of each class using f = [ligand]/([ligand] + Kd).
cards.back: Convert 1 nM to 1,000 pM. High-affinity occupancy = 100/(100 + 10) = 0.909, about 91%. Low-affinity occupancy = 100/(100 + 1,000) = 0.0909, about 9%.
cards.quote: fraction of sites occupied = [NGF] / ([NGF] + Kd)

cards.front: At 2 nM free ligand, calculate occupancy for sites with Kd = 10 pM, 1 nM and 2 nM. Use f = [ligand]/([ligand] + Kd). How does using the measured 2 nM low-affinity Kd change the rounded-model estimate?
cards.back: 10 pM = 0.010 nM: f = 2/(2 + 0.010) = 99.5%. For 1 nM: 2/(2 + 1) = 66.7%. For 2 nM: 2/(2 + 2) = 50%. The low-affinity estimate falls from about two-thirds to half.
cards.quote: 67% with the rounded 1 nM Kd, 50% with the measured 2 nM.

cards.front: Why can mature NGF act through p75 in a TrkA-lacking culture even though the simple binding model predicts greater fractional occupancy of high-affinity sites at low NGF?
cards.back: Nanomolar culture doses occupy many low-affinity p75 sites. At low concentrations, high-affinity sites are preferentially occupied.
cards.quote: At that level many p75-alone sites are occupied, which fits mature NGF acting through p75 in TrkA-lacking cells in a dish.

cards.front: Why can a simple ligand-binding occupancy calculation alone establish neither the number of bound receptors nor whether a cell survives?
cards.back: It gives the fraction occupied within each site class. Receptor abundance is needed for counts, and the model supplies no survival or death threshold.
cards.quote: The percentages are fractions of each class of site, not counts of receptors or strengths of signal,

cards.front: An NGF culture contains 50 ng/mL of free mature NGF (dimer molar mass 26.5 kDa). Convert this to nM, then calculate p75-alone occupancy using the rounded Kd = 1 nM and f = [NGF]/([NGF] + Kd). What makes this dose relevant to p75 experiments?
cards.back: 50 ng/mL = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ g/L; 26.5 kDa = 26,500 g/mol. Concentration = (5.0 × 10⁻⁵)/26,500 = 1.89 × 10⁻⁹ M, or 1.89 nM. Occupancy = 1.89/(1.89 + 1) ≈ 65%. Rule: nanomolar doses fill many p75 sites, allowing mature NGF to act through p75 in TrkA-lacking cultures; occupancy alone does not predict death.
cards.quote: Culture experiments often add NGF at around 50 nanograms per millilitre, which for a dimer of about 26.5 kilodaltons is about 2 nM.

cards.front: A researcher uses mature-NGF Kd values to predict that low-dose uncleavable proNGF cannot kill a p75–sortilin-rich cell. Why does that prediction fail?
cards.back: The mature-NGF model cannot decide precursor effects. Sortilin grips the pro-domain, enabling a different receptor interaction. Rules: ligand processing changes receptor engagement; the occupancy model supplies neither proNGF binding constants nor a death threshold.
cards.quote: This lesson puts no binding numbers on proNGF; its effects are compared by experiment instead.

cards.front: Two purified NGF batches behave differently. On a western blot, only the killing batch has a larger NGF-reactive band also recognized by a pro-domain antibody. What does that band identify?
cards.back: Uncut proNGF: the larger NGF-containing protein still carries its pro-domain.
cards.quote: If the killing batch carries a larger band that the pro-domain antibody recognises, it contains uncut proNGF.

cards.front: A proNGF-containing batch kills cells with p75 and sortilin but little TrkA. Design tests linking killing both to precursor processing and to the receptor pair.
cards.back: Block p75 and sortilin separately and test whether either blockade prevents killing. Add plasmin and track precursor conversion and killing activity. Loss of killing with conversion supports a processing explanation. Rules: the precursor’s pro-domain engages sortilin, and p75 with sortilin mediates death in these cells.
cards.quote: if the killing activity falls as the precursor band is converted to mature NGF, the difference between the batches was processing, not two different genes.

cards.front: Two developing neuron groups receive equal amounts of a target-derived survival factor, but one group dies more. Design a test of whether receptor availability accounts for the difference.
cards.back: Under matched factor exposure, compare receptor expression and restore the matching receptor in the poorly surviving group. Improved survival would support a receptor-dependent explanation. Rules: neurons need sufficient target-derived factor, and the receptors they express determine their response.
cards.quote: Both puzzles have one answer: the target supplies the factor, and the receptors give it its meaning.

cards.front: TrkA-expressing fibroblasts divide after NGF without p75. Does this settle whether neurons need a physical TrkA–p75 complex for high-affinity binding? What must a binding experiment address?
cards.back: No. Measure affinity with and without p75 in a matched cellular system; division alone does not establish a neuronal binding mechanism. Rules: TrkA sufficiency was shown in fibroblasts, and the mechanism of high-affinity cooperation remains disputed.
cards.quote: So the groups disagreed about binding itself, and the debate ran for years.
cards.section: The dispute over high-affinity NGF binding

cards.front: BDNF and NT-4 share which preferred Trk receptor?
cards.back: TrkB.
cards.quote: NT-4 was shown to act through TrkB soon after.
cards.section: How BDNF, NT-3, NT-4, TrkB and TrkC were found

cards.front: Does p75’s death domain mean it uses the same death signaling machinery as Fas?
cards.back: No. Fas uses FADD and caspase-8; p75 uses other adaptors and JNK activation.
cards.quote: p75's death domain is a family resemblance to Fas, not the same machinery.
cards.section: p75 and Fas: a family resemblance

cards.front: Why does development of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons in NGF-null mice fail to show that these neurons are unaffected by NGF dosage?
cards.back: Initial development and later neuronal condition differ: mice with one NGF gene copy show shrinkage of these neurons and poorer memory.
cards.quote: mice with one copy of the NGF gene show shrinkage of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and poorer memory.

cards.front: Why is developmental motor-neuron dependence on TrkB in mice described as unsettled?
cards.back: One TrkB-knockout study reported fewer motor neurons, but deleting both BDNF and NT-4 spared facial motor neurons.
cards.quote: mice lacking both TrkB ligands, BDNF and NT-4, kept their facial motor neurons, so whether motor neurons need TrkB during development is unsettled.

cards.front: Which experimental differences could help explain conflicting reports of proNGF-induced death and survival?
cards.back: Dose, receptor balance, precursor preparation and how much precursor was processed during the experiment.
cards.quote: Possible reasons include the dose, the cells' balance of receptors, how the precursor was prepared and how much of it was cut during the experiment.
